observation_kind: targeted current official polygon-capture, bulk-query, retired-LIDAR and terrain-metadata checks; not independent bulk HTTP fetches
rules: Overlapping polygons can be acceptable for different floor levels, strata, tenures and classes of title.
Caseworkers can classify acceptable overlaps and allow them to remain in the dataset.
System-referred index-polygon overlaps may be investigated and resolved by a caseworker.
Where registered title extents genuinely overlap, HMLR has limited power to amend them until an amendment or rectification application is received.
Minor index-polygon discrepancies are considered where registrations are intended to adjoin.
Some registered titles are correctly non-adjoining, so their index polygons should not meet.
An index polygon may be the same size, larger or smaller than the extent shown on the title plan.
Index polygons must not be relied upon to show the exact registered-title extent.
Historic index polygons were manually captured on OS county-series sheets, national-grid sheets and parcel books.
HMLR completed conversion of about 19 million paper index polygons to vector polygons in February 2004.
The 2004 vectorised polygons were mapped against Ordnance Survey Land-Line.
During the time-limited conversion, polygons were completed pictorially and title plans were seldom used to validate indexed extents.
HMLR's Positional Accuracy Improvement programme ran from 2005 to 2008.
Many affected polygons were moved automatically in sympathy with Ordnance Survey mapping.
Polygons outside the automated criteria were referred for manual comparison with the title plan.
Around 2009, nearly 14 million index polygons passed through the Quality Improvement Flowline.
The quality flow resolved some minor overlaps and automatically reconciled polygon extents with title plans.
Daily OS MasterMap change-only updates are used for new polygons and title plans rather than routine review of existing registrations.
Existing polygons are updated when title activity or an adjoining title requires a change.
Large-scale OS source mapping uses 1:1,250 urban, 1:2,500 semi-urban/rural and 1:10,000 mountain/moorland scales.
Footprint indexing captures the smallest building footprint that fully accommodates a title extent, which can be larger than the title itself.
Artificial footprints divide unusually large or complex multi-level developments into smaller index areas.
Exaggerated extents give narrow registered strips a displayed width of at least one metre.
Former gridding practice split polygons at national-grid sheet joins, sometimes creating several polygon IDs for one feature.
Former coextensive-leasehold practice sometimes captured a leasehold polygon to the freehold extent and was later discontinued.
Maintenance can be triggered by a customer query, an adjoining-registration problem, a noticed polygon error or a land sale requiring removal from a title.
Daily production changes are uploaded overnight to the publication environment and undergo simple validation.
Publication validation checks zero coordinates, zero-area polygons and duplicate coordinate points, and cleans many self-intersections.
Zero-area polygons and polygons below 0.1 square metres are removed from the publication environment.
A change-only update contains only the latest polygon version, previous versions are not retained, and the NPD is updated monthly.
Planning datasets can be downloaded in CSV, JSON and, where applicable, GeoJSON and Parquet formats.
The official documentation identifies Parquet as well suited to large datasets.
The Planning Data API remains in beta and may change for production systems.
Portfolio workflows are instructed to apply polite rate-limiting between per-property requests.
For hundreds of properties, bulk downloads support local spatial intersections and provide a stable snapshot.
Bulk-download URL formats vary by dataset and are listed on each dataset page.
The dataset-list endpoint provides an include_typologies boolean that can remove typologies when set to false.
A current title-boundary entity exposes entry/start/end dates, entity, dataset, typology, reference, prefix, organisation, geometry, point and quality, with HMLR and OS attribution under OGL.
The 25cm composite DTM product is retired and no longer available on the Data Services Platform.
The Environment Agency replaced the retired 25cm composite with a 1m-resolution composite.
The wider LIDAR archive still includes 25cm time-stamped survey data.
The retired product was a 2017 composite terrain model at 25cm spatial resolution.
It was derived by merging and resampling the Environment Agency's full time-stamped archive for coverage.
Where repeat surveys existed, the newest and best-resolution source was selected.
The retired composite was historically updated annually to incorporate newer surveys.
The 25cm terrain model was produced from the last-return LIDAR signal.
OS Terrain 50 XML metadata follows the GEMINI standard and is provided for national product sets and individual tiles.
The metadata processing date is the tile-creation date, not the real-world change or survey date.
Tile metadata records an incrementing publication version, a creation-or-revision reason and lineage describing new imagery, partial revision or verified no-change.
OS Terrain 50 is supplied as inert data and includes no software for manipulating it; GML may require translation for a GIS.
